records.source: Ἦν δὲ ἄνθρωπος ἐκ τῶν Φαρισαίων, Νικόδημος ὄνομα αὐτῷ, ἄρχων τῶν Ἰουδαίων·
records.gloss: Was now a man of the Pharisees, Nicodemus name to him, a ruler of the Jews;

L.1: Now there was a man of the Pharisees, Nicodemus [was] his name, a ruler of the Jews.

R.1: There was a man named Nicodemus. He was a Pharisee and one of the leaders of the Jewish people.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the Jewish people, among whom he was a leader
alternatives: the Jewish authorities as a group opposed to Jesus
decisions.reason: John uses the word in several senses (see the note on the book's terms). Here it names the people Nicodemus was a ruler of, so it means the Jewish people as a whole. Nicodemus himself is a Jew, as are Jesus and his disciples.

decisions.choice: a ruler: one of the leading men of the nation, most likely a member of the council in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: In John the "rulers" are the leading men in Jerusalem, named alongside the Pharisees (7:26, 48; 12:42). In 7:50-51 Nicodemus speaks up among the chief priests and Pharisees when they meet in council, so he belonged to the governing body of the Jews in Jerusalem, which met under the high priest.

decisions.choice: Pharisees: the movement devoted to keeping the law exactly
decisions.reason: See the note at 1:24. The Pharisees had already questioned John the Baptist (1:24-25); now one of them comes to Jesus.

decisions.choice: a man: the story continues from 2:24-25
alternatives: a new story with no link to what comes before
decisions.reason: Chapter 2 ended with Jesus knowing "what was in man" (2:25), using the same word. John opens with "a man" and "now", so Nicodemus comes as one example of the people of 2:23-25 whose belief rested on signs (3:2).

decisions.choice: Nicodemus [was] his name
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Greek way of giving a name ("Nicodemus, name to him") and brackets the verb English needs.

decisions.choice: one of the leaders of the Jewish people
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say plainly what "ruler" means and name the people he led (meaning decisions m1 and m2). Literal keeps the word John wrote.

records.heading: Jesus and Nicodemus

records.source: οὗτος ἦλθεν πρὸς αὐτὸν νυκτὸς καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Ῥαββί, οἴδαμεν ὅτι ἀπὸ θεοῦ ἐλήλυθας διδάσκαλος· οὐδεὶς γὰρ δύναται ταῦτα τὰ σημεῖα ποιεῖν ἃ σὺ ποιεῖς, ἐὰν μὴ ᾖ ὁ θεὸς μετ’ αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: This one came to him by night and said to him, "Rabbi, we know that from God you have come [as] teacher; no one for is able these the signs to do which you do, if not may be the God with him."

L.2: He came to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} by night and said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Rabbi, we know that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have come from God [as a] teacher; for no one is able to do these signs that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} do, unless God is with {{gender:them|him}}."

R.2: One night he came to see Jesus. He said, "Rabbi, we know that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are a teacher God has sent. No one could do the signs {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} do unless God was with {{gender:them|him}}."

decisions.choice: by night: a plain note of time that John also gives a deeper sense
alternatives: a sign that Nicodemus came in secret, out of fear
a quiet time chosen for a long talk
decisions.reason: John recalls the detail twice (19:39, "who had first come to him by night"), so it matters to him. Rulers who believed were afraid to say so openly (12:42), which suggests secrecy, but the text does not give a motive. In this Gospel night and darkness stand for life away from the light (1:5; 9:4; 11:10; 13:30, "and it was night"), and the talk ends with people who come to the light or stay away from it (3:19-21). Every level keeps "at night" and draws no conclusion about his reasons.

decisions.choice: we know: Nicodemus speaks for others too
alternatives: a polite plural for himself alone
decisions.reason: The plural suggests he speaks for a group, perhaps fellow Pharisees or the people of 2:23 who believed when they saw his signs. Jesus answers in the plural in 3:7 and 3:11-12.

decisions.choice: signs: the deeds of 2:23 that point to who Jesus is
decisions.reason: Key term. Nicodemus draws a right but limited conclusion from the signs: God must be with this teacher (compare 9:16, 33). John has just said that belief based only on signs is not enough (2:23-25); Jesus's answer moves to what Nicodemus does not yet see.

decisions.choice: Rabbi: a respectful title for a teacher
decisions.reason: See the note at 1:38. A ruler and a known teacher (3:10) gives this title to a teacher without formal training (compare 7:15), and so honors him.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Jesus, since the last person named was Nicodemus.

decisions.choice: {{gender:them|him}}
decisions.reason: "No one ... unless God is with him" is a general rule about anyone, so the gender setting applies. The pronoun is not about Jesus, so it is not a deity pronoun.

decisions.choice: a teacher God has sent
alternatives: have come from God as a teacher
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "come from God" means here.

records.source: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω σοι, ἐὰν μή τις γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν, οὐ δύναται ἰδεῖν τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ.
records.gloss: Answered Jesus and said to him, "Amen, amen I say to you, if not someone be born from above, not he is able to see the kingdom of the God."

L.3: Jesus answered and said to him, "Truly, truly I say to you, unless {{gender:someone|a man}} is born from above, {{gender:they|he}} cannot see the kingdom of God."

R.3: Jesus answered, "I tell you the truth: no one can see God's kingdom unless God gives {{gender:them|him}} a new birth from above."

decisions.choice: from above, with "again" also in view: a double meaning that Nicodemus hears only one way
decisions.reason: ἄνωθεν can mean "from above" (3:31; 19:11; 19:23, of a robe woven from the top) or "again, anew" (Galatians 4:9). Everywhere else in John it means from above, and the birth Jesus describes comes from God (1:13) and from the Spirit (3:5-8). Nicodemus hears "a second time" (3:4). Both senses are true of what Jesus means: a new birth that comes from God. The other side: "again" is the familiar rendering and fits Nicodemus's reply, and some early readers took it so.

decisions.choice: the kingdom of God: God's rule and the life of the age to come
decisions.reason: This phrase is common in Matthew, Mark and Luke but appears in John only here and in 3:5. In the rest of the conversation Jesus speaks instead of eternal life (3:15-16, 36), which is John's usual way of describing the same gift.

decisions.choice: see: experience, have a part in
decisions.reason: To "see" the kingdom is to share in it; 3:5 says "enter", and 3:36 speaks of "seeing life" in the same way.

decisions.choice: Jesus answers the question behind Nicodemus's words
decisions.reason: Nicodemus has not asked anything. Jesus replies to what lies behind his opening, as one who knows what is in a person (2:25): seeing signs is not enough to see God's kingdom.

decisions.choice: anyone, man or woman
decisions.reason: τις is general, so the gender setting applies.

decisions.choice: Truly, truly I say to you (L); Truly, truly, I tell you (B); I tell you the truth (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide rendering for John (see 1:51), recorded once in this passage; it covers 3:5 and 3:11 as well.

decisions.choice: born from above
decisions.reason: No single word carries both senses of the Greek (meaning decision m1). Literal and Balanced give the sense John uses elsewhere; it departs from the familiar "born again", so the footnote gives that rendering.

decisions.choice: unless God gives them a new birth from above
alternatives: unless they are born from above
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the one who gives the birth, which "from above" means (1:13), and says "a new birth from above" so that both senses of the word are kept. The order is turned round so the sentence is simpler.

decisions.choice: {{gender:someone|a man}} ... {{gender:they|he}}
decisions.reason: Inclusive default; the traditional form one tap away.

records.source: λέγει πρὸς αὐτὸν ὁ Νικόδημος· Πῶς δύναται ἄνθρωπος γεννηθῆναι γέρων ὤν;
records.gloss: Says to him the Nicodemus, "How is able a man to be born old being?

L.4: Nicodemus says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "How is a man able to be born, being old?

R.4: Nicodemus asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "How can a man who is already old be born?

decisions.choice: a man who is old: Nicodemus puts the question in his own case
decisions.reason: The question is general in form, but γέρων is the word for an old man, and the next sentence speaks of "his mother". Nicodemus is thinking of a man like himself, so the gender setting is not used.

decisions.choice: he takes "born" in the physical sense
alternatives: he understands and objects on purpose
decisions.reason: John often lets a hearer take Jesus's words on the wrong level, then lets Jesus explain (2:20-21; 4:11, 15; 6:52; 11:11-13). Nicodemus heard only "born again" and thinks of a second natural birth (the next sentence).

decisions.choice: said / asked
decisions.reason: John often tells a story in the present tense ("says") for vividness. Literal keeps it; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told. This applies throughout the passage.

records.source: μὴ δύναται εἰς τὴν κοιλίαν τῆς μητρὸς αὐτοῦ δεύτερον εἰσελθεῖν καὶ γεννηθῆναι;
records.gloss: Not is he able into the womb of the mother of him a second time to enter and to be born?"

L.4: He cannot enter into the womb of his mother a second time and be born, can he?"

R.4: He cannot go back inside his mother and be born a second time!"

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer no
decisions.reason: μὴ at the start of the question shows that Nicodemus expects "no": the idea seems absurd to him.

decisions.choice: a second time: he heard Jesus's word as "again"
decisions.reason: "A second time" shows how Nicodemus understood the word in 3:3 (meaning decision m1 there).

decisions.choice: an exclamation
decisions.reason: Readable turns a question that expects "no" into the statement it implies, so that young readers do not miss the point.

records.source: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς· Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω σοι, ἐὰν μή τις γεννηθῇ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ πνεύματος, οὐ δύναται εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ.
records.gloss: Answered Jesus, "Amen, amen I say to you, if not someone be born of water and Spirit, not he is able to enter into the kingdom of the God.

L.5: Jesus answered, "Truly, truly I say to you, unless {{gender:someone|a man}} is born of water and Spirit, {{gender:they|he}} cannot enter into the kingdom of God.

R.5: Jesus answered, "I tell you the truth: no one can enter God's kingdom unless {{gender:they are|he is}} born of water and the Spirit.

decisions.choice: water and Spirit: one birth with two sides, cleansing and new life from God
alternatives: water stands for baptism, and the Spirit for the gift that comes with it
water stands for natural birth, and the Spirit for the second birth
decisions.reason: One preposition governs both nouns, so they describe a single birth. The prophets promised that God would wash his people with clean water and put his Spirit within them (Ezekiel 36:25-27), and a teacher of Israel should know this (3:10). Baptism is also close at hand: John has baptized with water and promised one who baptizes with the Spirit (1:26, 33), and baptism follows in 3:22-26. Some take the water as natural birth (compare 3:6), but a single phrase for two different births is unlikely. Every level keeps "water and the Spirit" without explaining it.

decisions.choice: Spirit: the Holy Spirit
decisions.reason: There is no article, but the Spirit here is the one who gives the birth (3:6, 8), the Spirit who came down on Jesus (1:32-33).

decisions.choice: the same saying as 3:3, explained
decisions.reason: "Born from above" becomes "born of water and the Spirit", and "see" becomes "enter". The second saying tells Nicodemus what kind of birth he meant: not a second natural birth, but one God gives.

decisions.choice: the Spirit
decisions.reason: English needs the article for the Holy Spirit; Literal keeps the Greek without it.

decisions.choice: {{gender:someone|a man}} ... {{gender:they|he}}
decisions.reason: As in 3:3.

records.source: τὸ γεγεννημένον ἐκ τῆς σαρκὸς σάρξ ἐστιν, καὶ τὸ γεγεννημένον ἐκ τοῦ πνεύματος πνεῦμά ἐστιν.
records.gloss: The [thing] having been born of the flesh flesh is, and the [thing] having been born of the Spirit spirit is.

L.6: What has been born of the flesh is flesh, and what has been born of the Spirit is spirit.

R.6: Human parents give their children a human life. But those who are born of the Spirit have the Spirit's life.

decisions.choice: flesh: human nature, weak and mortal, as it comes by natural birth
decisions.reason: In John σάρξ means ordinary human existence (1:13-14, "the Word became flesh"; 6:63; 17:2), not sin as often in Paul. Natural birth gives natural life; it cannot produce the life of God's kingdom.

decisions.choice: the Spirit (the Holy Spirit) gives spirit (a life that belongs to God)
decisions.reason: The first is the Holy Spirit, who gives the birth (3:5). The second names what is born: a life of the Spirit's own kind (compare 4:24; 6:63). Like produces like.

decisions.choice: a general rule: whatever is born
decisions.reason: The neuter "what is born" states a principle that covers every person.

decisions.choice: Whatever is born
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the general rule in plain words.

decisions.choice: Human parents give their children a human life ... the Spirit's life
alternatives: What is born of the flesh is flesh
decisions.reason: "Flesh is flesh" means little to young readers; Readable says what natural birth gives and what the Spirit gives (meaning decisions m1 and m2).

records.source: μὴ θαυμάσῃς ὅτι εἶπόν σοι Δεῖ ὑμᾶς γεννηθῆναι ἄνωθεν.
records.gloss: Not do marvel that I said to you, 'It is necessary for you [all] to be born from above.'

L.7: Do not marvel that I said to you, 'It is necessary for you [all] to be born from above.'

R.7: Do not be surprised that I said, 'All of you need a new birth from above.'

decisions.choice: "to you" is singular, then "you" is plural: the need is for everyone
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks to Nicodemus (singular), but the saying is for all, including those Nicodemus spoke for with his "we know" (3:2).

decisions.choice: from above, as in 3:3
decisions.reason: See meaning decision m1 at 3:3.

decisions.choice: must: a necessity, not advice
decisions.reason: The same word is used of the Son of Man in 3:14 and of John in 3:30: it is what God's purpose requires.

decisions.choice: [all] (L); All of you (B, R)
decisions.reason: English "you" does not show the plural (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: be surprised
decisions.reason: Everyday words; Literal keeps "marvel".

records.source: τὸ πνεῦμα ὅπου θέλει πνεῖ, καὶ τὴν φωνὴν αὐτοῦ ἀκούεις, ἀλλ’ οὐκ οἶδας πόθεν ἔρχεται καὶ ποῦ ὑπάγει· οὕτως ἐστὶν πᾶς ὁ γεγεννημένος ἐκ τοῦ πνεύματος.
records.gloss: The wind where it wills blows, and the sound of it you hear, but not you know from where it comes and where it goes; thus is everyone the [one] having been born of the Spirit.

L.8: The wind blows where it wills, and its sound you hear, but you do not know from where it comes and where it goes; so is everyone who has been born of the Spirit."

R.8: The wind blows wherever it wants. You can hear it, but you cannot tell where it started or where it will go. It is like that with everyone who is born of the Spirit."

decisions.choice: wind and Spirit: one word, with a play on its two senses
decisions.reason: πνεῦμα means both wind (or breath) and spirit; the verb "blows" comes from the same root. Jesus speaks of the wind and means the Spirit as well, as Ezekiel's vision plays on wind, breath and Spirit giving life to dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9-14). The footnote shows that the two words are one.

decisions.choice: sound, which can also mean voice
decisions.reason: The word is the ordinary one for sound or voice: the wind's sound is heard, as the Spirit's work is known by its effects.

decisions.choice: the birth from the Spirit is real, free and beyond human control
alternatives: the person born of the Spirit becomes unpredictable
decisions.reason: As no one controls or tracks the wind but its effects are plain, so it is with the Spirit's work in those he gives birth to. The point is not that such people behave strangely, but that their birth comes from God, not from human doing (1:13).

decisions.choice: wind ... Spirit
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John: one word cannot carry both senses here, so the first is "wind" and the last is "Spirit", with the footnote (meaning decision m1). "It" refers to the wind; the Spirit is never called "it".

decisions.choice: where it wills
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the verb of wanting; Balanced and Readable use "wants".

records.source: ἀπεκρίθη Νικόδημος καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Πῶς δύναται ταῦτα γενέσθαι;
records.gloss: Answered Nicodemus and said to him, "How are able these things to happen?"

L.9: Nicodemus answered and said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "How can these things happen?"

decisions.choice: these things: the birth from the Spirit Jesus has described
decisions.reason: Nicodemus no longer argues; he asks how. These are his last words in the chapter. He returns in 7:50-51, when he defends Jesus before the council, and in 19:39, when he brings spices for Jesus's burial.

decisions.choice: this
decisions.reason: English refers to one matter with a singular word.

records.source: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Σὺ εἶ ὁ διδάσκαλος τοῦ Ἰσραὴλ καὶ ταῦτα οὐ γινώσκεις;
records.gloss: Answered Jesus and said to him, "You are the teacher of the Israel and these things not you know?

L.10: Jesus answered and said to him, "You are the teacher of Israel, and you do not know these things?

R.10: Jesus answered, "You are an important teacher of Israel, and you still do not understand this?

decisions.choice: the teacher of Israel: a well-known teacher, perhaps said with some irony
alternatives: a teacher of Israel, one among many
the one chief teacher of the nation
decisions.reason: The article marks Nicodemus as a recognized teacher. He had greeted Jesus as "a teacher come from God" (3:2); now Jesus turns the title back on him.

decisions.choice: a teacher of Israel should have known it from the Scriptures
decisions.reason: The prophets had spoken of God giving a new heart and his Spirit within his people (Ezekiel 36:25-27; Jeremiah 31:33). Jesus is not teaching something unheard of in Israel.

decisions.choice: know: understand
decisions.reason: The verb means to know with understanding; Nicodemus has heard the words but not grasped them.

decisions.choice: an important teacher
decisions.reason: Readable says what the article implies (meaning decision m1).

records.source: ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω σοι ὅτι ὃ οἴδαμεν λαλοῦμεν καὶ ὃ ἑωράκαμεν μαρτυροῦμεν, καὶ τὴν μαρτυρίαν ἡμῶν οὐ λαμβάνετε.
records.gloss: Amen, amen I say to you that what we know we speak and what we have seen we testify, and the testimony of us not you [all] receive.

L.11: Truly, truly I say to you, what we know we speak, and what we have seen we testify [to], and our testimony you [all] do not receive.

R.11: I tell you the truth: we talk about what we know, and we tell about what we have seen. But you people do not accept what we say.

decisions.choice: we: Jesus speaks in the plural, and who is included is not clear
alternatives: Jesus and John the Baptist, both witnesses
a reply in kind to Nicodemus's "we know"
decisions.reason: Jesus switches from "I" to "we" and back to "I" (3:12). He may be answering Nicodemus's "we know" (3:2) with a "we" of his own, or joining others who testify, as the Father and John do (5:31-37). The text does not say, so every level keeps "we".

decisions.choice: you: plural, Nicodemus and those he speaks for
decisions.reason: "I say to you" is singular, but "you do not receive" is plural, as in 3:7.

decisions.choice: testify, testimony: witness given as evidence, as in a court
decisions.reason: The words of 1:7 and 1:19. Jesus speaks of what he knows firsthand, as a witness does; to "receive" his testimony is to accept it as true (3:32-33; compare 1:11-12).

decisions.choice: you people
decisions.reason: Shows the plural (meaning decision m2); Literal uses [all].

records.source: εἰ τὰ ἐπίγεια εἶπον ὑμῖν καὶ οὐ πιστεύετε, πῶς ἐὰν εἴπω ὑμῖν τὰ ἐπουράνια πιστεύσετε;
records.gloss: If the earthly things I told you [all] and not you believe, how if I tell you the heavenly things will you believe?

L.12: If earthly things I told you [all] and you do not believe, how, if I tell you heavenly things, will you believe?

R.12: I have told you about things that happen here on earth, and you do not believe. So how will you believe if I tell you about the things of heaven?

decisions.choice: earthly things: what happens on earth, such as the new birth; heavenly things: what belongs to God's own realm
alternatives: earthly things are things told in earthly pictures (birth, wind)
earthly things are ordinary, unimportant matters
decisions.reason: The new birth happens to people here on earth, and Jesus has explained it with earthly pictures. The heavenly things are what follows: the Son of Man who came down from heaven, his lifting up, and God's love in giving him (3:13-16).

decisions.choice: the first "if" states a fact: you do not believe
decisions.reason: The first condition describes what is actually happening; the second looks ahead to what Jesus is about to say.

decisions.choice: believe: accept what he says as true
decisions.reason: Key term. Here the verb has no "in": the question is whether they believe his words (compare 2:22).

records.source: καὶ οὐδεὶς ἀναβέβηκεν εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν εἰ μὴ ὁ ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ καταβάς, ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου.
records.gloss: And no one has gone up into the heaven except the [one] out of the heaven having come down, the Son of the Man.

L.13: And no one has gone up into heaven except the one who came down out of heaven, the Son of Man.

R.13: No one has ever gone up into heaven except the Son of Man. He is the one who came down from heaven.

decisions.choice: only the one who came down from heaven can speak of heavenly things
alternatives: spoken from after Jesus's ascension: no one has gone up except the Son of Man, who first came down
decisions.reason: The sentence answers 3:12: no one has gone up to heaven and come back to tell of it; only the one who came down from there knows heavenly things (compare 1:18). The perfect "has gone up" can also be read as looking back from after Jesus's return to the Father (6:62; 20:17), which would suit the view that from here on the evangelist is speaking (see 3:16). Every level keeps the plain wording.

decisions.choice: Proverbs 30:4 and Deuteronomy 30:12
decisions.reason: "Who has gone up to heaven and come down?" (Proverbs 30:4) asks who can know God's ways; Deuteronomy 30:12 says the law is not in heaven, that someone must go up to fetch it. Jesus's answer is that the one who knows heaven has come down from it.

decisions.choice: the Son of Man: Jesus's title for himself, here as the one from heaven
decisions.reason: See the note at 1:51. In John the Son of Man has come down from heaven (6:62) and will be lifted up (3:14; 8:28; 12:34).

decisions.choice: ends with "the Son of Man" (SBLGNT)
alternatives: adds "who is in heaven" (many later manuscripts)
adds "who was in heaven" (a few early translations)
decisions.reason: The papyri P66 and P75 and Codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus end the verse with "the Son of Man". Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add "who is in heaven"; a few versions read "who was in heaven". Some have defended the longer reading as the harder one. The footnote gives it. A reviewer should check this note against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: gone up ... came down
decisions.reason: The same plain verbs as in 1:51 ("going up and coming down"), so the link between the two sayings stays visible.

records.source: καὶ καθὼς Μωϋσῆς ὕψωσεν τὸν ὄφιν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ, οὕτως ὑψωθῆναι δεῖ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, ἵνα πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων ἐν αὐτῷ ἔχῃ ζωὴν αἰώνιον.
records.gloss: And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, thus to be lifted up it is necessary the Son of the Man, \v 15 so that everyone the [one] believing in him may have life eternal.

L.14: And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so it is necessary for the Son of Man to be lifted up,
L.15: so that everyone who believes may in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} have eternal life.

R.14: Long ago in the desert, Moses lifted up a bronze snake on a pole. In the same way, the Son of Man must be lifted up,
R.15: so that everyone who believes can have eternal life in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}: the life of the age to come, which begins now.

decisions.choice: the bronze serpent of Numbers 21:8-9
decisions.reason: When poisonous snakes struck the people in the wilderness, God told Moses to make a serpent and set it on a pole; Moses made it of bronze, and anyone who had been bitten and looked at it lived (Numbers 21:4-9). As looking at the lifted serpent brought life, so believing in the lifted-up Son of Man brings eternal life.

decisions.choice: lifted up: raised on the cross, and by that exalted
decisions.reason: ὑψωθῆναι is used of raising something high and of exalting someone. John says plainly that it points to the way Jesus would die (12:32-33), and 8:28 and 12:34 use it the same way. In the Greek of Isaiah 52:13 the LORD's servant "will be lifted up and glorified". The cross is where Jesus is raised up and where he is glorified, so every level keeps "lifted up" with both senses.

decisions.choice: must: what God's purpose requires
decisions.reason: As in 3:7 and 3:30. The lifting up is not an accident but part of God's plan.

decisions.choice: in him goes with "have eternal life": eternal life is found in him
alternatives: in him goes with "believes": everyone who believes in him
decisions.reason: Elsewhere John always writes "believe in" with a different preposition (3:16, 18, 36), never with this one. So "in him" most likely goes with "may have eternal life": the life is in him (1:4; 20:31; 1 John 5:11). But the words stand right after "believes", and some read "believes in him". The meaning is close either way.

decisions.choice: everyone who believes may have eternal life in him (SBLGNT)
alternatives: everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add "should not perish, but" from verse 16, and some change the preposition to the usual one for "believe in". The shorter text has the oldest witnesses. A reviewer should check this note against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: eternal life: the life of the age to come, God's own life, which begins now
decisions.reason: Key term. The word for eternal belongs to "the age" to come; John stresses that believers have this life already (3:36; 5:24) and defines it as knowing God and Jesus Christ whom he sent (17:3).

decisions.choice: Long ago ... a bronze snake on a pole
decisions.reason: Readable says what the serpent was and how it was lifted up (Numbers 21:9), which readers need to follow the comparison.

decisions.choice: lifted up, with no "on the cross"
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John keeps "lifted up" at every level. Readable could add "on a cross", but that would lose the exaltation; the comparison with the snake on a pole already makes the picture clear.

decisions.choice: Moses lifted up ..., and in the same way
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the comparison but states the first half as a plain sentence.

decisions.choice: who believes may in him have eternal life
alternatives: who believes in him may have eternal life
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Greek order and shows that "in him" goes with having life (meaning decision m4).

decisions.choice: the life of the age to come, which begins now
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John lets Readable explain eternal life once in a passage (meaning decision m6).

decisions.choice: serpent (B); snake (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the older word used in the story of Numbers 21; Readable uses the everyday word.

records.source: Οὕτως γὰρ ἠγάπησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν κόσμον ὥστε τὸν υἱὸν τὸν μονογενῆ ἔδωκεν, ἵνα πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων εἰς αὐτὸν μὴ ἀπόληται ἀλλὰ ἔχῃ ζωὴν αἰώνιον.
records.gloss: Thus for loved the God the world, so that the Son the only [one] he gave, so that everyone the [one] believing in him not may perish but may have life eternal.

L.16: For in this way God loved the world, that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} gave the Son, the one and only, in order that everyone who believes in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} may not perish but may have eternal life.

R.16: God loved the people of the world, and this is how {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} loved them: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} gave {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} one and only Son, so that everyone who believes in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} will not be lost but will have eternal life.

decisions.choice: Jesus's words to Nicodemus continue to the end of 3:21
alternatives: Jesus's words end at 3:15, and 3:16-21 is the evangelist's own reflection
decisions.reason: The manuscripts have no quotation marks, so where the quotation ends is a judgment. Nothing in the text marks a break: 3:16 begins with "For", which ties it to 3:14-15, and the themes run on (the Son, believing, eternal life). On the other side, the verbs move to the past ("loved", "gave"), Nicodemus is not addressed again, and "the one and only Son" and "believe in the name" are the evangelist's own phrases elsewhere (1:12, 14, 18; 1 John 4:9). Every level keeps the quotation open to 3:21; the footnote gives the other view. 3:31-36 raises the same question.

decisions.choice: in this way: God's love took the form of giving the Son
alternatives: so much: God loved the world to such a degree
decisions.reason: Οὕτως normally means "thus, in this way" in John (3:8; 4:6; 21:1), and it has just been used in 3:14: "so must the Son of Man be lifted up". "For" links the two: this is how God loved the world, by giving the Son to be lifted up. ὥστε with the past tense states what actually happened: he gave. 1 John 4:9 makes the same point: "in this the love of God was revealed, that God sent his one and only Son." The other side: the greatness of the love is plain from what it gave, and the familiar "so loved" is often heard as "loved so much".

decisions.choice: the world: humanity, which has turned from God
decisions.reason: Key term. As in 1:10 and 1:29, the world here is humanity as a whole, which did not know its maker (1:10) and loves darkness (3:19). That God loves this world is the surprise.

decisions.choice: one and only, unique
decisions.reason: As in 1:14 and 1:18: μονογενής means unique, the only one of his kind, not "begotten" (see meaning decision m4 at 1:14). The footnote gives the familiar "only begotten".

decisions.choice: possibly an echo of Abraham and Isaac (Genesis 22)
decisions.reason: God told Abraham, "Take your son, your only son, whom you love" (Genesis 22:2), and praised him for not holding back his son (22:12, 16). Here God himself gives his one and only Son. John does not draw the link, so it is uncertain.

decisions.choice: gave: sent into the world and gave up to death
decisions.reason: The next verse says God "sent" the Son; 3:14 has just spoken of his lifting up. The giving includes both (compare Romans 8:32; Galatians 1:4).

decisions.choice: perish: be lost, destroyed, the opposite of eternal life
decisions.reason: The same verb is used of being lost (6:39; 10:28; 17:12). Believers still die (11:25); what they are spared is final ruin.

decisions.choice: "the Son" (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts add "his"; some of the oldest do not. The meaning is the same, so no footnote. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: in this way God loved the world, that (L); God's love for the world was such that (B)
alternatives: God so loved the world that
God loved the world so much that
decisions.reason: Literal gives the sense of the adverb (meaning decision m2). In Balanced, "such" can mean "of this kind" or "so great", which keeps the open question in meaning decision m2 without leaning to degree, as "so much" does. It departs from the familiar "so loved".

decisions.choice: his one and only Son
decisions.reason: English needs a possessive here; the Son is God's. Literal keeps "the Son".

decisions.choice: the people of the world ... this is how he loved them
alternatives: God loved the world in this way
decisions.reason: Readable says who the world is (meaning decision m3) and spells out "in this way".

decisions.choice: be lost
decisions.reason: "Perish" is an uncommon word for young readers; "be lost" is how John uses the verb elsewhere (meaning decision m7).

decisions.choice: everyone who believes, with no gender setting
decisions.reason: The Greek is general and the wording is already inclusive; no pronoun for the believer is needed, so no setting applies.

L.17: For God did not send the Son into the world in order that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} might judge the world, but in order that the world might be saved through {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.17: God did not send {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son into the world to judge it guilty. He sent {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} so that the world could be saved through {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: judge: pass sentence on, condemn
decisions.reason: Set against "be saved", the verb here means a judgment that goes against someone. Jesus does bring judgment (5:22, 27; 9:39), but it is not the purpose of his coming (12:47).

decisions.choice: the world: humanity, as in 3:16
decisions.reason: Key term. The word comes three times in one sentence: the whole world is the object of God's saving purpose.

decisions.choice: be saved through him: God saves, the Son is the one through whom
decisions.reason: The passive points to God as the one who saves; "through him" names the Son as the means. The Samaritans call Jesus "the Savior of the world" (4:42).

decisions.choice: sent: the Son comes on the Father's mission
decisions.reason: John often calls God "the one who sent me" (5:24; 6:38-39); the Son acts for the Father who sent him.

decisions.choice: condemn (B); judge it guilty (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "judge" so the word family of 3:17-19 can be seen; Balanced and Readable give its sense here (meaning decision m1).

R.21: But anyone who lives by the truth comes to the light. Then it becomes clear that what {{gender:they have|he has}} done was done in union with God."

decisions.choice: do the truth: act faithfully, live by what is true
decisions.reason: A Hebrew way of speaking: to "do truth" is to act faithfully (Genesis 47:29; Nehemiah 9:33). 1 John 1:6 uses it the same way. It is the opposite of doing evil (3:20).

decisions.choice: done in God: done in fellowship with God, by his working
alternatives: done in the sight of God
decisions.reason: "In God" in John describes a life lived in union with God (14:10, 20; 17:21). Such deeds come from God, so the one who does them is not afraid to have them seen.

decisions.choice: revealed: made visible
decisions.reason: The same verb as in 1:31 and 2:11, where Jesus and his glory are revealed.

decisions.choice: Jesus's words end here

decisions.choice: practices the truth (B); lives by the truth (R)

decisions.choice: {{gender:their|his}}; {{gender:they have|he has}}
decisions.reason: As in 3:20.

decisions.reason: Aenon means "springs". In the early 300s Eusebius placed it in the Jordan valley about eight Roman miles south of Scythopolis (Beth-shan), near Salim. decisions.reason: The plural suggests several springs; John baptized by immersion, so he needed a good supply.

R.24: This was before John was put in prison.

decisions.choice: ritual cleansing (B); the washings that made people clean for worship (R)
decisions.reason: Says what kind of purification is meant (meaning decision m3).

records.source: ὁ ἔχων τὴν νύμφην νυμφίος ἐστίν· ὁ δὲ φίλος τοῦ νυμφίου ὁ ἑστηκὼς καὶ ἀκούων αὐτοῦ, χαρᾷ χαίρει διὰ τὴν φωνὴν τοῦ νυμφίου.
records.gloss: The [one] having the bride bridegroom is; the now friend of the bridegroom, the [one] standing and hearing him, with joy rejoices because of the voice of the bridegroom.

L.29: The one who has the bride is [the] bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom's voice.

R.29: The bride is for the bridegroom. The bridegroom's friend stands nearby and listens for him, and when he hears the bridegroom's voice, his heart is full of joy.

decisions.choice: the friend of the bridegroom: the groom's close friend who helped him at the wedding
decisions.reason: At a Jewish wedding a close friend of the groom acted for him, helping to arrange the marriage and attending him at the feast. His part was to serve the groom, not to take the bride.

decisions.choice: the bridegroom and the bride: a picture of God and his people
decisions.reason: The prophets picture the LORD as Israel's husband (Isaiah 54:5; 62:4-5; Hosea 2:16-20). In the Gospels Jesus speaks of himself as the bridegroom (Mark 2:19-20), and Revelation calls God's people the bride of the Lamb (Revelation 21:2, 9). Here Jesus is the bridegroom, the people who come to him are the bride, and John is the friend.

decisions.choice: rejoices with joy: rejoices greatly
decisions.reason: Joining a verb to its own noun is a Hebrew way of adding force.

decisions.choice: stands and hears him: waits ready for the groom and listens to him
decisions.reason: The friend stands by to serve and is glad to hear the groom's voice, perhaps when the groom arrives to claim his bride.

decisions.choice: rejoices with joy (L); rejoices with great joy (B)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the doubled words; Balanced keeps the key term "joy" and shows the added force (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: him, with no deity_pronoun setting
decisions.reason: Within the picture the pronoun refers to the bridegroom of the story, not directly to Christ, so it is written plainly.

decisions.choice: The bride is for the bridegroom
alternatives: The one who has the bride is the bridegroom
decisions.reason: Readable says the point plainly: the bride belongs to the groom, not to his friend.

records.source: αὕτη οὖν ἡ χαρὰ ἡ ἐμὴ πεπλήρωται.
records.gloss: This therefore the joy the mine has been fulfilled.

L.29: So this joy of mine has been fulfilled.

R.29: That is the joy I have, and now it is complete.

decisions.choice: has been fulfilled: made full and stays full
decisions.reason: The perfect passive says John's joy has reached its fullness and remains so. Jesus uses the same words of his disciples' joy (15:11; 16:24; 17:13).

decisions.choice: John's joy is that people are coming to Jesus
decisions.reason: What troubled his disciples (3:26) is the very thing that makes John glad: the bride is going to the bridegroom.

records.source: ἐκεῖνον δεῖ αὐξάνειν, ἐμὲ δὲ ἐλαττοῦσθαι.
records.gloss: That one it is necessary to increase, me but to decrease.

L.30: That one must increase, but I must decrease.

R.30: He must become more and more important, while I become less and less.

decisions.choice: must: what God's purpose requires
decisions.reason: The same word as in 3:7 and 3:14. John accepts his lessening as part of God's plan, not as a loss to resent.

decisions.choice: increase, decrease: grow in honor and following, and grow less
decisions.reason: The verbs describe growth and shrinking; here they apply to standing among the people. John's whole testimony points away from himself to Jesus (1:20, 27, 30).

decisions.choice: He
decisions.reason: English uses a plain pronoun; at the start of a sentence it is capitalized either way.

decisions.choice: become more and more important ... less and less
decisions.reason: Readable says what the increase and decrease are (meaning decision m2).

records.source: Ὁ ἄνωθεν ἐρχόμενος ἐπάνω πάντων ἐστίν.
records.gloss: The [one] from above coming above all is.

L.31: The one who comes from above is above all.

R.31: The one who comes from above is greater than everyone.

decisions.choice: John the Baptist's words continue to the end of 3:36
alternatives: John's words end at 3:30, and 3:31-36 is the evangelist's own reflection
3:31-36 are words of Jesus, moved from elsewhere
decisions.reason: The manuscripts have no quotation marks. Nothing in the text marks a new speaker, and 3:31 explains why "he must increase": he comes from above. On the other side, the speech moves from "I" to statements about the one from heaven, and the language is close to Jesus's own in 3:11-13 and to the evangelist's in 3:16-21. Every level keeps the quotation open to 3:36, as with 3:16-21; the footnote gives the other view.

decisions.choice: from above: from heaven, as the next sentence says
decisions.reason: This is ἄνωθεν, the word of 3:3 and 3:7. Here it can only mean "from above"; it shows the sense the word has had in the whole chapter.

decisions.choice: above all: over all people, and over all things
decisions.reason: "All" may be people (set against "the one from the earth") or all things (compare 3:35). Both are true.

decisions.choice: greater than all (B); greater than everyone (R)
decisions.reason: "Above all" can be heard as "most of all"; Balanced and Readable say what it means.

records.heading: The one who comes from above

records.source: ὁ ὢν ἐκ τῆς γῆς ἐκ τῆς γῆς ἐστιν καὶ ἐκ τῆς γῆς λαλεῖ· ὁ ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἐρχόμενος ἐπάνω πάντων ἐστίν·
records.gloss: The [one] being from the earth from the earth is and from the earth speaks; the [one] from the heaven coming above all is;
pieces: from an earthly point of view

L.31: The one who is from the earth is from the earth and speaks from the earth; the one who comes from heaven is above all.

R.31: Anyone who comes from the earth belongs to the earth and speaks as someone from the earth. But the one who comes from heaven is greater than everyone.

decisions.choice: the one from the earth: any merely human messenger, John included
decisions.reason: The contrast is about origin, not truth: John is from the earth and speaks as a man of the earth, though he was sent by God (1:6). The one from heaven speaks of what he has seen there (3:32).

decisions.choice: the second "is above all" (SBLGNT)
alternatives: without it: the one who comes from heaven testifies to what he has seen and heard (some early manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Some early witnesses, among them the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Bezae, leave out the repeated "is above all" and join the clause to 3:32. The meaning is much the same, so no footnote. A reviewer should check this note against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: speaks from an earthly point of view
decisions.reason: Says what speaking "from the earth" means (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: greater than all / everyone
decisions.reason: As in the previous sentence.

records.source: ὃ ἑώρακεν καὶ ἤκουσεν τοῦτο μαρτυρεῖ, καὶ τὴν μαρτυρίαν αὐτοῦ οὐδεὶς λαμβάνει.
records.gloss: What he has seen and heard, this he testifies, and the testimony of him no one receives.

L.32: What {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has seen and heard, this {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} testifies, and no one receives {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} testimony.

R.32: He tells what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has seen and heard, but no one accepts what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says.

decisions.choice: he speaks from what he has seen and heard with the Father
decisions.reason: The one from heaven is an eyewitness of God (1:18; 3:11; 8:26, 38). His witness is firsthand.

decisions.choice: no one: hardly anyone, an overstatement
decisions.reason: Like "his own did not receive him" (1:11), this is a sweeping statement; the next verse speaks of those who do receive it (compare 1:12).

decisions.choice: testimony, receive: as in 3:11
bears witness to
decisions.reason: Varies the verb so that "testimony" can follow; the Greek words are related.

records.source: ὁ λαβὼν αὐτοῦ τὴν μαρτυρίαν ἐσφράγισεν ὅτι ὁ θεὸς ἀληθής ἐστιν.
records.gloss: The [one] having received his the testimony has sealed that the God true is.

L.33: The one who has received {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} testimony has sealed [the fact] that God is true.

R.33: But those who do accept what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says confirm that God is true to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} word.

decisions.choice: set a seal: confirm as genuine
decisions.reason: A seal pressed on a document showed that it was authentic and agreed to (1 Kings 21:8; Esther 8:8; Jeremiah 32:10). To accept the testimony is to put one's own seal to it.

decisions.choice: accepting the Son's words means affirming that God speaks truly
decisions.reason: The one God sent speaks God's own words (the next verse), so whoever accepts them declares that God is true; refusing them treats God as a liar (1 John 5:10).

decisions.choice: true: truthful, reliable
decisions.reason: The adjective describes one whose word can be trusted.

decisions.choice: {{gender:their|his}}
decisions.reason: The person meant is anyone; inclusive default. Literal needs no pronoun and Readable uses the plural.

decisions.choice: has sealed [the fact] that
alternatives: has set his seal to this
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the single verb and brackets the object English needs.

decisions.choice: But those who do accept ... confirm that God is true to his word
alternatives: has set his seal that God is true
decisions.reason: Readable explains the image of the seal (meaning decision m1) and the sense of "true" (m3), and shows the contrast with the previous sentence.

records.source: ὃν γὰρ ἀπέστειλεν ὁ θεὸς τὰ ῥήματα τοῦ θεοῦ λαλεῖ, οὐ γὰρ ἐκ μέτρου δίδωσιν τὸ πνεῦμα.
records.gloss: Whom for sent the God the words of the God he speaks, not for from measure he gives the Spirit.

L.34: For the one whom God sent speaks the words of God, for not by measure does {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} give the Spirit.

R.34: The one God sent speaks God's words, because the Spirit is given without any limit.

decisions.choice: who gives the Spirit is not stated: most likely God gives the Spirit to the Son without limit
alternatives: the Son gives the Spirit to believers without limit
God gives the Spirit to believers without limit
decisions.reason: The verb has no subject. The nearest subject is God, and the next verse says the Father has given all things into the Son's hand; the Spirit came down on Jesus and remained (1:32-33; Isaiah 11:2). This explains why he speaks God's words. Many later manuscripts add "God" as the subject. On the other side, the present tense "gives" can describe Jesus, who baptizes with the Spirit and gives the Spirit (1:33; 7:39; 20:22). Every level keeps the open wording; the footnote gives both readings.

decisions.choice: the Spirit: the Holy Spirit
the one God sent: the Son, who speaks God's words
decisions.reason: John often calls Jesus the one the Father sent (3:17; 5:36-38), and Jesus says his teaching is not his own but the Father's (7:16; 12:49; 14:10).

decisions.choice: not by measure: without limit, not rationed out
decisions.reason: A measure was a fixed amount; the Spirit is given in full.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: The giver is God or the Son (meaning decision m1); either way the pronoun takes the deity_pronoun setting.

decisions.choice: the Spirit is given without any limit
alternatives: he gives the Spirit without measure
decisions.reason: Readable uses the passive, so that like the Greek it does not name the giver, and avoids a "he" young readers might take one way only.

records.source: ὁ πατὴρ ἀγαπᾷ τὸν υἱόν, καὶ πάντα δέδωκεν ἐν τῇ χειρὶ αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: The Father loves the Son, and all things has given into the hand of him.

L.35: The Father loves the Son, and all things {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has given into {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hand.

R.35: The Father loves the Son and has given {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} power over everything.

decisions.choice: the Father's love for the Son
decisions.reason: John uses both verbs for love of the Father's love for the Son (here and 5:20); see the note on the book's terms. This love is the ground of all the Son has (17:24).

decisions.choice: into his hand: under his authority and care
decisions.reason: To give something into someone's hand is to put it in their power (13:3; 17:2; compare Matthew 28:18).

decisions.choice: has given: the gift stands
decisions.reason: The perfect tense describes a gift made and still in force.

decisions.choice: has handed everything over to him
alternatives: has given all things into his hand
decisions.reason: Plain wording for the idiom (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: has given him power over everything
decisions.reason: Readable says what the idiom means (meaning decision m2).

records.source: ὁ πιστεύων εἰς τὸν υἱὸν ἔχει ζωὴν αἰώνιον· ὁ δὲ ἀπειθῶν τῷ υἱῷ οὐκ ὄψεται ζωήν, ἀλλ’ ἡ ὀργὴ τοῦ θεοῦ μένει ἐπ’ αὐτόν.
records.gloss: The [one] believing in the Son has life eternal; the [one] but disobeying the Son not will see life, but the wrath of the God remains on him.

L.36: The one who believes in the Son has eternal life; but the one who disobeys the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains on {{gender:them|him}}."

R.36: Anyone who believes in the Son has eternal life already. But anyone who does not obey the Son will not have that life. Instead, God's anger remains on {{gender:them|him}}."

decisions.choice: disobey, refuse to obey: the opposite of believing
decisions.reason: ἀπειθῶν means to disobey or refuse to be persuaded. John sets it against "believes": not believing the Son is disobeying him, refusing the claim God makes through him. The sense includes unbelief, and it has often been rendered "does not believe"; the footnote gives that.

decisions.choice: has: eternal life is a present possession
decisions.reason: Key term. The believer already has eternal life (5:24); compare 3:18, where the unbeliever is already judged.

decisions.choice: see life: experience it, share in it
decisions.reason: As "see the kingdom of God" in 3:3.

decisions.choice: the wrath of God: God's settled opposition to evil and his judgment on it
decisions.reason: The word is used only here in John. It is not a sudden temper but God's just response to the refusal of his Son (Romans 1:18).

decisions.choice: remains: it is already on them and stays
decisions.reason: The present tense matches "already judged" in 3:18. μένει is John's word "remain"; the one who believes is taken out from under the wrath, and the one who refuses stays under it.

decisions.choice: disobeys (L); refuses to obey (B); does not obey (R)
decisions.reason: Every level keeps the sense of obeying (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: remains
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John: "remain" for this verb in its weighty sense.

decisions.choice: God's anger
decisions.reason: "Wrath" is an uncommon word for young readers; "anger" is the plain word, explained in meaning decision m4.

decisions.choice: already; will not have that life
alternatives: has eternal life; will not see life
decisions.reason: Readable shows that the life is present now (meaning decision m2) and gives the sense of "see" (m3).

decisions.choice: {{gender:them|him}}
decisions.reason: The person meant is anyone who refuses; inclusive default.
